searchText: Ugh. When will software engineers learn to not give time estimates? And when will the world learn to ignore all estimates from software engineers? The answer is blowing in the wind 😄 > Ugh. When will software engineers learn to not give time estimates? <@301186049323958275> when project managers who are under pressure to deliver stop asking for them? 😉 "Danny said that deployment had been pushed back slightly to allow the audit of the Blst crypto library to be completed first. I don’t know why this was a blocker as neither the deposit contract nor the official deposit tooling use that library." So why was it a blocker? <@301186049323958275> Which s/w engineers are giving time estimates? The one in the screenshot above, I forget who it was. Also, all of software engineers in all of history. 😖 That screenshot is from my newsletter, and I definitely ain't a software engineer 😂 I feel like it ultimately comes down to type of business as well, a software bug on spotify frustrates me for a bit, a software bug on ethereum makes me never trust the currency again. So I agree with Micah that making promises is bad business in crypto. And yet, dates still matter... How so? I have some responsibility for coordinating all the Eth2 activities at ConsenSys - this involves not a few people, not a few moving parts, and a fair amount of planning. Being in limbo is a programme manager's nightmare. Besides - we (the community) are ready (imho, as product owner of one of the clients). Let's do this thing. I agree with the sentiment. Though, I guess what I'm saying isn't that having goal dates to hit is bad, but promising those dates to stake holders is I can appreciate a desire to get something "finished" or otherwise reach a milestone. That doesn't mean that you should ignore decades of evidence that programmers and project managers making date estimates about software projects has like a 90% failure rate. But we're there - it isn't even a prediction at this point: maybe an expression of frustration that nobody pulled the trigger yet. I feel like maybe a better thing would be to break the large task into a bunch of smaller ones and then let stake holders know when those smaller pieces are complete -- then the stake holders have a rough idea of how progress is coming along, but without being told an arbitrary stamp of completion such as "in 2020" > But we're there - it isn't even a prediction at this point: maybe an expression of frustration that nobody pulled the trigger yet. <@!573787335796326400> We aren't "there", else the date would be in the past. 🙂 Also, not too sure about the details of eth2 so I'll step out now. Can anyone just launch the contract? I suppose it's on github right, so someone just needs to publish it? > Can anyone just launch the contract? <@!276099850918166529> They can launch _a_ contract. The address of the contract used by the chain is part of its specification, so just creating a contract at an arbitrary address won't do any good. v1 spec isn't out yet right? so the v1 spec can put the address after Yes, but the general point is that random people creating deposit contracts won't help because until the address is enshrined in the specification there is no way of knowing if sending Ether to the contract will result in a valid deposit or your funds disappearing in to the void. In principle one or more client teams could deploy the contract, make a release and start the chain. It's permissionless, right?, which is kind of the point. But far better to move forward together in step 🙂 If client teams are ready, then why wouldn't it be together in step? Guess anon can just publish it, put up some reddit post, and if upvoted then it's launched :P v1 spec then can go out within minutes with the address > In principle one or more client teams could deploy the contract, make a release and start the chain. It's permissionless, right?, which is kind of the point. But far better to move forward together in step 🙂 <@!573787335796326400> Kind-of a pre-genesis hard fork There is no such thing as "official" tooling. Blst is by far the most performant library and is integrated into almost all clients as the default choice Only last week did lighthouse strip out the ability to make deposits on their client. Not sure about the rest It is and will be an incredibly prominent bls library for all things bls. One of those bls things is creating and verifying deposits (Lighthouse link, 10 days ago -- https://github.com/sigp/lighthouse/pull/1780) We marked our deposit tooling as deprecated in Teku 3 weeks ago (https://github.com/ConsenSys/teku/pull/2919) and plan to disable it before the deposit contract is deployed (https://github.com/ConsenSys/teku/issues/2876). Will the deposit contract be launched next week? Same here. Prysm has removed its deposit tooling 4 weeks ago. https://github.com/prysmaticlabs/prysm/pull/7379 "This PR removes the prysm deposit command, instead favoring users to try the official eth2.0-deposit-cli which is actively maintained and kept updated." I guess that uses BLSt? The officially unofficial eth2.0-deposit-cli does not use Blst. Right, so is this just a matter of the EF guys not being updated on what clients have done in regards to this particular aspect then? Or more how to launch this in a decentralized way where no one can be held responsible? I think this was an effort from everyone to help promote Launchpad and reduce confusion Hopefully the client tutorials are ready for once that launchpad gets to command line Guess need to raise awareness as well in light of the eth1 BLS fork not going through for many more months now. I’ve noticed that the narrative around ETH in ETH2 being listed as a separate asset come Phase 0 is picking up. Has anyone evaluated the potential risk of this from an economic incentives perspective and willingness to validate if there is no price peg between what I imagine will be ETH and some ticker for Beacon Chain ETH? I understand exchanges may not list it specifically as the asset itself is locked on the Beacon chain, but I assume some derivatives will emerge As a user, not affiliated with any client efforts, "we are ready" may be right for Teku, but when I look at Prysm, it needs to bake in Medalla's heat some more. Just today it fell over (can't deliver attestations successfully all the time, only some of the time) once the exit queue grew. I fully expect it'll be in much better shape a week from now, and even better shape a week after that. And, that's been the story for that particular client ever since day 2 of non-finality. To be clear: The Prysm team is doing amazing work and the client from `master` today is nothing like the client on Oct 13th. So much progress. And - it needs a few more weeks of that progress, and then it needs to prove itself stable.
